rationale: B wins because it knows where the facts stop. A's "Canva bought an AI image startup, then shipped it as a brand-safety feature" turns an unproven product link into the headline, then tries to launder it in the proof list. B's "The two are supplied as separate facts; the link between them is unconfirmed" is the adult move, and it still gives the founder usable doors into competitive, SaaS-metrics, finance, and enterprise-AI coverage.
gaps_in_A: "Canva bought an AI image startup, then shipped it as a brand-safety feature" invents the causal link the update does not give you. The proof list admits the gap, but the headline already blew it.
"24,000 paid teams, 220 million users — and Canva can't name one enterprise customer" overstates "not disclosed" into "can't name." That is a small wording choice with a libelous little aftertaste.
"Design tools are becoming compliance software" stretches SSO/admin/brand controls into compliance without evidence of audit logs, retention, data residency, or security review.
"The acquisition and the AI generation feature land together" is too neat. The update says "recently acquired" and "launching"; it does not say the acquisition powers this launch.
gaps_in_B: "funding-mechanics" is the wrong label. There is no funding event, secondary sale, IPO signal, or financing mechanism here; call it a private-company business-model angle.
"choosing to move upmarket is a capital-markets question" is viable but thin without valuation source, revenue mix, or an on-record finance rationale.

"Why IT admins should care about Canva's single sign-on" — `duplicate` is too quick. The SSO/admin/brand-control bundle can support a distinct CIO/procurement angle if scoped to governance instead of product review.
"large user base moving its sales motion into accounts the incumbents already own" needs a named customer or displacement example before it is more than competitive posture.
